content: Have you ever seen a cloth that looks like a beautiful painting with bright colours and geometric patterns? Imagine a whole village where almost every family works together to make these magical cloths! Let's travel to a special town in Telangana.
How do you think a simple white cotton or silk thread turns into a colourful saree with complex designs? Do they paint the cloth after weaving, or is there a secret hidden in the threads themselves?

content.title: The Secret of the Threads
content.description: Before weaving, the threads are carefully tied in specific places and dipped in colours. Watch how the pattern appears on the threads!

content: The magic happens in Pochampalli! The threads are first tied in specific patterns and then dyed in bright colours. This process is called Ikat. After drying, they are rolled into bundles and woven on handlooms to create world-famous Pochampalli sarees.

description: A machine operated by hand or foot (without electricity) used for weaving cloth.
A traditional technique of tying and dyeing yarn before it is woven into cloth.

question: What is the special process of tying and dyeing threads before weaving called?

content: Why do you think the weavers need to be very careful while tying and dyeing the threads? If even one thread is tied wrongly, the entire design on the saree will be ruined! Think about the precision required.

Just like Pochampalli sarees, there are many other traditional crafts in India, like Kullu shawls from Himachal Pradesh, Madhubani paintings from Bihar, and Assam silk. Each craft tells a story about its region's culture and history.
Design your own pattern! If you were a Pochampalli weaver, what geometric shapes and colours would you use for your cloth? Draw your Ikat design on a piece of paper!

Making a Pochampalli cloth takes many days of hard work by the whole family. But sadly, many weavers are leaving this beautiful craft and moving to cities to work as labourers. Why do you think this is happening?
If a Pochampalli saree is sold for a lot of money in big city shops, who do you think gets most of that money? The weaver who worked day and night, or the big shopkeeper?

content.title: The Journey of Profit
content.description: Notice how the middleman and big shopkeeper take the largest share of the money, leaving very little for the weaver.

content: Weavers get very little money for their hard work. Silk thread is becoming very expensive, and middlemen or big shopkeepers take most of the profit. This makes it hard for weavers to survive and feed their families.

description: A person who buys goods from producers and sells them to shopkeepers or consumers, often taking a large profit.

question: Why are many weavers giving up their traditional craft?
options: Because they don't like making cloth anymore
Because silk is expensive and they get very little money

content: How would you feel if you worked for a whole month to make something beautiful, but someone else took all the reward?

This problem is not just for weavers. Many farmers and artisans in India face the same problem where middlemen take the profit. This is why buying directly from artisans helps them more and saves our heritage.
Imagine you are running a campaign to save the Pochampalli craft. Write a short catchy slogan to encourage people to buy directly from the weavers and support their art!
Discuss with students what they can do to support local artisans in their own city or state.
Students often think machine-made cloth is better because it's cheaper. Remind them that handmade crafts like Pochampalli carry unique art, tradition, and quality that machines cannot copy.
